Getting started with heimdall

Source: vignettes/heimdall.Rmd
heimdall.Rmd

Heimdall detects concept drift in data streams: moments when the data, or the relationship between the data and the target, stop behaving as they did before. This vignette shows the workflow shared by every detector in the package and when to use each family of detectors.

library(daltoolbox)
library(heimdall)

Real and virtual concept drift

Heimdall distinguishes two kinds of change:

  • Real concept drift changes the relationship between the inputs and the target. It is visible in the errors of a predictive model, so it is monitored with error-based detectors: dfr_ddm(), dfr_eddm(), dfr_hddm(), dfr_ecdd() and dfr_cusum(). They receive 1 for a wrong prediction and 0 for a correct one.
  • Virtual concept drift changes the distribution of the inputs, whether or not the model is affected. It is monitored with distribution-based detectors, which look at a numeric feature directly: dfr_adwin(), dfr_kswin(), dfr_kldist(), dfr_mcdd(), dfr_lbdd() and dfr_page_hinkley(). dfr_aedd() does the same for several features at once.

The streaming contract

Every detector follows the same three rules:

  1. update_state(obj, value) processes one observation and returns a list with the updated detector (obj) and a flag (drift) telling whether a drift was detected in that call;
  2. obj$drifted is sticky: it stays TRUE after the first detection;
  3. reset_state(obj) returns the detector to its initial state, usually right after a drift has been handled.

The loop below is the canonical way of running a detector over a stream. It works unchanged for any detector in the package.

detect <- function(model, stream) {
  output <- list(obj = model, drift = FALSE)
  drifts <- integer(0)
  for (i in seq_along(stream)) {
    output <- update_state(output$obj, stream[i])
    if (output$drift) {
      drifts <- c(drifts, i)
      output$obj <- reset_state(output$obj)
    }
  }
  drifts
}

Virtual drift: monitoring a feature

st_drift_examples$univariate is a synthetic series whose behaviour changes at the observations flagged in the event column. ADWIN keeps a window of adaptive size and shrinks it whenever its older and newer parts have significantly different means.

data(st_drift_examples)
serie <- st_drift_examples$univariate

drifts <- detect(dfr_adwin(), serie$serie)
drifts
#> [1] 224 352 448
plot(serie$serie, type = "l", col = "grey40", xlab = "observation", ylab = "serie")
abline(v = which(serie$event), lty = 2, col = "grey70")
abline(v = drifts, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomleft", c("true change", "detection"), lty = c(2, 1),
       col = c("grey70", "firebrick"), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

Real drift: monitoring the errors of a model

Error-based detectors only need the sequence of mistakes of a model. Here the error rate jumps from 10% to 40% at observation 501.

set.seed(42)
errors <- c(rbinom(500, 1, 0.1), rbinom(500, 1, 0.4))

detect(dfr_ddm(), errors)
#> [1] 576
detect(dfr_hddm(), errors)
#> [1] 560
plot(cumsum(errors) / seq_along(errors), type = "l", xlab = "observation",
     ylab = "cumulative error rate")
abline(v = 500, lty = 2, col = "grey70")
abline(v = detect(dfr_ddm(), errors), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

Processing a whole batch

When there is no need to react to each observation, fit() feeds a whole batch to the detector and returns the updated object. Because drifted is sticky, it tells whether a drift happened anywhere in the batch.

model <- fit(dfr_ddm(), errors)
model$drifted
#> [1] TRUE

Combining detectors

dfr_multi_criteria() combines several distribution-based detectors. With combination = "or" any detector can raise the alarm, with "and" all of them must report a drift within fuzzy_window observations, and "fuzzy" weighs each detection by how recent it is. model$detections counts the alarms of each detector.

model <- dfr_multi_criteria(
  drifter_list = list(adwin = dfr_adwin(), ph = dfr_page_hinkley()),
  combination = "or"
)
model <- fit(model, data.frame(serie = serie$serie))
model$drifted
#> [1] TRUE
model$detections
#> adwin    ph 
#>     6     1

Baselines

dfr_inactive() never reports a drift and dfr_passive() always does. They are useful as lower and upper references when evaluating how a model adapts.
